intro: The Ramayana is one of the best-loved stories in the world. It tells of Prince Rama, his wife Sita, his brother Lakshmana and their loyal helper Hanuman. Hindu tradition honors the sage Valmiki as its first poet.

In this unit you will follow the whole story, from the palace in Ayodhya to the forest, to Lanka and home again. You will see how the poem teaches dharma, doing what is right for your role. You will also see how readers ask hard questions and tell the story in many new ways.
By the end, you will be able to retell the main events in order. You will be able to explain dharma with examples. You will be able to compare two tellings of the Ramayana fairly.
bigQuestion: What does the Ramayana teach about doing what is right, and why do people tell it in so many ways?

title: The Ramayana

chapters.title: Valmiki's Poem: From Ayodhya to the Forest
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it mean to do what is right for your role?

story.title: Sandals on the Throne
story.kicker: A brother carries a pair of sandals home and sets them on an empty throne.
paragraphs: Prince Bharata walks slowly back into the city of Ayodhya. His eyes are red from crying. In his hands he carries something small. It is a pair of wooden sandals.
The sandals belong to his older brother, Rama. Rama has gone to live in the forest for fourteen years. Everyone says Bharata should be king now. The people wait to see what he will do.
Bharata climbs the steps to the great hall. He does not sit on the throne. Instead, he kneels down. Carefully, he places Rama's sandals on the seat. The hall is silent.
"These sandals will rule," he tells the court. "I will only take care of the kingdom for my brother. When Rama comes home, the throne is his." Then he bows to the sandals.
The people are quiet. Then some begin to cry too. They have never seen a prince turn down a crown. Many Hindus still tell this story as a picture of loyalty and doing what is right.
story.think: Bharata could have been king. Why do you think he put the sandals on the throne instead?

sections.title: The First Poet and His Poem

lessons.title: Valmiki, the First Poet
lessons.mainIdea: Hindu tradition honors Valmiki as the first poet and the author of the Ramayana.
reading: Hindu tradition calls *Valmiki* the adi kavi, which means "the first poet." Tradition says he made the Ramayana in Sanskrit. The poem tells the life of Prince Rama.
The poem itself tells how Valmiki began. He saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds. The other bird cried out in grief. Valmiki felt deep sorrow, and his words came out in a new rhythm.
Tradition says that rhythm became the shloka, the verse form of the whole poem. So, the story goes, poetry was born from sorrow and care for another living thing.

words.d: the sage whom Hindu tradition honors as the first poet and author of the Ramayana
a verse form with a steady rhythm, used in the Ramayana

look.title: Poetry Born From Grief
look.text: Valmiki sees a hunter kill one of two birds. Its mate cries out. Valmiki's sorrow pours out as a curse on the hunter, spoken in a new, even rhythm. He is surprised by his own words.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Book 1), canto 2
look.prompt: What feeling does the poem say started Valmiki's poetry?

check.why: Tradition calls Valmiki the adi kavi, the first poet.

check.q: What did Valmiki see before he spoke his first verse?

check.why: Bala Kanda tells of the hunter and the pair of birds.

check.q: What is a shloka?

lessons.title: Seven Books
lessons.mainIdea: Valmiki's Ramayana has seven books, called kandas, and about 24,000 verses.
reading: Valmiki's Ramayana is divided into seven books. Each book is called a *kanda*. Each kanda tells one part of Rama's life, from his childhood to the end of his reign.
The poem has about 24,000 verses, by the traditional count. That is very long. It would take many days to chant it all. Many families read a small part at a time.
The names of the books tell where the story happens. Ayodhya Kanda happens in Rama's city. Aranya Kanda happens in the forest. Sundara Kanda, the "beautiful book," follows Hanuman to Lanka.

words.d: one of the seven books of the Ramayana
a line or small group of lines in a poem

look.title: The Seven Kandas
look.cite: Valmiki's Ramayana; book names as in Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki (1870–74)
look.prompt: In which book does the battle happen?

check.q: What is a kanda?
choices: One of the seven books of the Ramayana
check.why: The Ramayana has seven books called kandas.

check.q: About how many verses does the Ramayana have?
check.why: The traditional count is about 24,000 verses.

check.q: Which kanda follows Hanuman to Lanka?
check.why: Sundara Kanda, the fifth book, follows Hanuman.

lessons.title: How Old Is the Ramayana?
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition and scholars give different dates for the Ramayana.
reading: Hindu tradition places Rama's life in a very ancient age of the world, called the Treta Yuga. Many Hindus believe Rama lived long, long ago, far earlier than written history.
Scholars look at the poem's language and its history. Most date Valmiki's poem to between about 500 BCE and 100 CE. Many think the first and last books were added later.
Both views are held today. A student can name both without choosing between them. You might say, "Tradition says..." and then, "Scholars date..." Both are part of learning.

words.d: beliefs and practices handed down over time
a person who studies a subject very carefully

look.title: Two Answers to One Question
look.text: A student asks, "How old is the Ramayana?" Her grandmother says Rama lived in a very ancient age. Her teacher says scholars date the poem to about 500 BCE to 100 CE. Both answers are shared with care.
look.prompt: How can you report both answers fairly in one sentence?

check.q: In which age does tradition place Rama?
check.why: Hindu tradition places Rama in the Treta Yuga.

check.q: How do most scholars date Valmiki's poem?
check.why: Most scholars date it between about 500 BCE and 100 CE.

check.q: What is a fair way to report both views?
choices: Say what tradition holds and what scholars date
Say only one view is allowed
check.why: A fair report names both the traditional view and the scholarly date.

lessons.title: A King and Four Sons
lessons.mainIdea: King Dasharatha of Ayodhya has four sons, and Rama is the eldest.
reading: The Ramayana begins in *Ayodhya*, a rich city in North India. Its king is Dasharatha. He is a good king, but for many years he has no children. He prays and waits.
At last, the poem says, his three queens have four sons. Queen Kausalya's son is Rama. Queen Kaikeyi's son is Bharata. Queen Sumitra has twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
Rama is the eldest. He grows up brave, kind and wise. He marries Sita, a princess from the kingdom of Mithila. The king plans to make Rama the next ruler.

words.d: Rama's home city in the Ramayana
the king of Ayodhya and Rama's father

look.title: Dasharatha's Family
look.prompt: Which queen had twins?

check.q: Who is Rama's father?
check.why: Dasharatha, king of Ayodhya, is Rama's father.

check.q: Who is Bharata's mother?
check.why: Bharata is Kaikeyi's son.

check.q: Where is Sita from?
check.why: Sita is a princess of Mithila.

lessons.title: Kaikeyi's Two Wishes
lessons.mainIdea: Queen Kaikeyi uses two old promises to change who will be king.
reading: Long before, Queen Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha's life in a battle. He promised her two wishes, called boons. She could ask for them any time. He never forgot that promise.
Now Rama is about to be crowned. Kaikeyi's maid, Manthara, stirs up her fears. Kaikeyi goes to the king. She asks for her two boons at last. Manthara tells Kaikeyi her son will lose everything.
First, she wants her son Bharata to be king. Second, she wants Rama sent to the forest for fourteen years. The king is heartbroken. But he gave his word, and he cannot take it back.

words.d: a wish or gift promised to someone
being sent away from your home

look.title: A Hard Promise
look.text: Dasharatha loves Rama very much. He also gave his word to Kaikeyi long ago. If he breaks his promise, he is not a truthful king. If he keeps it, he loses his son.
look.prompt: What two good things are pulling against each other for the king?

check.q: Why did the king owe Kaikeyi two boons?
check.why: Kaikeyi saved Dasharatha in battle, and he promised her two boons.

check.q: What is a boon?
check.why: A boon is a wish someone has promised to grant.

check.q: What was Kaikeyi's second wish?
choices: Rama sent to the forest for fourteen years
check.why: She asked for Rama's exile for fourteen years.

lessons.title: Rama Chooses Exile
lessons.mainIdea: Rama accepts exile calmly so that his father's word is kept.
reading: Rama hears the news. He does not argue. He does not get angry. The poem shows him accepting the exile calmly, so that his father's promise is kept. He says he is ready to go.
Sita insists on coming with him. She says a wife's place is at her husband's side. Lakshmana insists on coming too, to serve and protect his brother. Neither one will stay behind.
The three leave Ayodhya in simple clothes made of bark. The people weep. Soon after, King Dasharatha dies of grief. Many readers see this as one of the saddest parts of the poem.

words.d: to agree to something, even if it is hard
deep sadness, especially after a loss

look.title: Rama's Answer
look.text: Rama tells Kaikeyi he is glad to go to the forest to keep his father's word. He says he would do even more to honor his father's promise.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Book 2)
look.prompt: Why do you think the poem shows Rama as calm, not angry?

check.q: How does Rama react to the news?
check.why: Ayodhya Kanda shows Rama accepting exile calmly.

check.q: Who goes with Rama into exile?
check.why: Sita and Lakshmana choose to go with Rama.

check.q: What happens to King Dasharatha?
check.why: The poem says the king dies of grief after Rama leaves.

lessons.title: Bharata's Choice
lessons.mainIdea: Bharata refuses the throne and rules in Rama's name, with Rama's sandals on the throne.
reading: Bharata was away when all this happened. When he comes home, he is shocked. He does not want a crown won this way. He goes to the forest to bring Rama back.
Rama says no. He must keep his father's word. So Bharata asks for Rama's sandals. He carries them home and places them on the throne. Rama agrees and blesses him.
Bharata rules for fourteen years as Rama's stand-in. The poem says he lives simply, outside the city, waiting for his brother. Many Hindus honor Bharata as a model of a loyal brother.

words.d: staying true to someone or something
a person who takes someone's place for a while

look.title: What the Sandals Mean
look.text: A pair of sandals sits on a golden throne. No one sits there. Every day, Bharata makes decisions in Rama's name. The sandals remind everyone who the true king is.
look.prompt: What do the sandals stand for in this part of the story?

check.q: What does Bharata place on the throne?
check.why: Bharata places Rama's sandals on the throne.

check.q: Why does Bharata go to the forest?
check.why: Bharata wants Rama to come home and rule.

check.q: How do many Hindus see Bharata?
choices: As a model of a loyal brother
check.why: Many Hindus honor Bharata's loyalty to Rama.

lessons.title: Sages and Simple Living
lessons.mainIdea: In the forest, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana live simply and meet wise sages.
reading: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk deep into the forests of India. They build huts of leaves and branches. They eat fruit and roots. They live very simply.
In the forest, they meet many sages. A sage is a wise person who lives a holy life. The sages welcome them and teach them. Some ask Rama to protect them from danger.
The poem describes rivers, flowers, birds and changing seasons. Many readers love these nature scenes. Some of the places named in the poem are still pilgrimage sites today.

words.d: a wise person who lives a holy life
a journey to a holy place

look.title: A Day in the Forest
look.text: At dawn, Sita gathers flowers by the river. Lakshmana brings water and wood. Rama visits a sage who lives nearby. In the evening, they sit by a small fire and listen to the birds.
look.prompt: How is this life different from life in a palace?

check.q: What is a sage?
choices: A wise person who lives a holy life
check.why: Sages are wise people who live holy lives.

check.q: How do Rama, Sita and Lakshmana live in the forest?
check.why: They build simple huts and live on fruit and roots.

check.q: What is a pilgrimage?
choices: A journey to a holy place
check.why: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place.

lessons.title: Dharma: Right for Your Role
lessons.mainIdea: In the Ramayana, dharma means doing what is right for your role in life.
reading: The Ramayana is full of a key word: *dharma*. In this story, dharma means doing what is right for your role. A son, a brother, a wife and a king each have duties.
Rama keeps his father's word. Bharata protects his brother's throne. Lakshmana serves his brother. Sita stays true to Rama. Many Hindus see each one as a model of dharma.
Dharma is not always easy. Sometimes two duties pull against each other, like the king's love for his son and his promise. The Ramayana shows people facing these hard choices.

words.d: duty, or the right way to live for your role in life
something you should do because of your role

look.title: Four People, Four Duties
rows: Bharata guards the throne for Rama
look.prompt: Pick one person. What role is that person living up to?

check.q: What does dharma mean in the Ramayana?
choices: Doing what is right for your role
check.why: In the Ramayana, dharma means doing right for your role.

check.q: How does Rama show dharma?
choices: He takes the throne by force
check.why: Rama keeps his father's promise.

check.q: Why is dharma sometimes hard?
choices: Two duties can pull against each other
check.why: The poem shows duties that clash, like the king's love and his promise.

lessons.title: Tulsidas Tells It Again
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1500s, the poet Tulsidas retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi.
reading: Valmiki's poem is in Sanskrit. Most people in North India did not speak Sanskrit. In the 1500s, the poet *Tulsidas* retold the story in Awadhi, a form of Hindi.
His poem is called the Ramcharitmanas, "the lake of Rama's deeds." Tulsidas was a devoted follower of Rama. His telling is full of love for Rama as God.
The Ramcharitmanas became one of the most loved books in North India. Families chant it at home and in temples. Many Hindus in Illinois know its verses by heart.

words.d: the poet who retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi in the 1500s
full of love and loyalty

look.title: Two Tellings Side by Side
look.text: Valmiki tells Rama's story as a great epic about a noble prince. Tulsidas, many centuries later, tells it as a song of devotion to Rama as God. Both tell the same events. Each has its own feeling.
look.prompt: Why might a poet retell a story that people already know?

check.q: Who retold the Ramayana in a form of Hindi?
check.why: Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a form of Hindi.

check.q: When did Tulsidas write?
check.why: Tulsidas wrote in the 1500s.

check.q: What feeling fills the Ramcharitmanas?
check.why: Tulsidas writes with deep devotion to Rama.

review.q: Whom does Hindu tradition call the first poet?
review.why: Tradition calls Valmiki the adi kavi, the first poet.

review.q: How many kandas does the Ramayana have?

choices: Bharata as king and Rama's exile
review.why: Kaikeyi used her two boons for Bharata's crown and Rama's exile.
Rama is exiled for fourteen years.

review.q: What does Bharata put on the throne?
review.why: Bharata sets Rama's sandals on the throne and rules in his name.

review.q: What does dharma mean in the Ramayana?
choices: Doing what is right for your role
review.why: In the Ramayana, dharma is right action for your role.

review.q: How do most scholars date Valmiki's poem?
review.why: Most scholars date it between about 500 BCE and 100 CE.
The Ramcharitmanas is Tulsidas's retelling in a form of Hindi.

chapters.title: Lanka, Return and the Meaning of Dharma
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people keep retelling the Ramayana, and why do their tellings differ?

story.title: Ten Nights of the Ramayana
story.kicker: A town in India puts on the whole Ramayana as a play that lasts ten nights.
paragraphs: In a small town in North India, the autumn air is cool. Every evening, people carry mats and blankets to an open field. Strings of lights hang above a wooden stage.

This is the Ramlila, a play of Rama's life. Each night the town acts out a new part. On the first night, Rama is born. On another night, he leaves for the forest. The crowd grows bigger every evening.
The actors are neighbors: a shopkeeper, a teacher, some boys from the high school. Children in the front row know the lines by heart. They whisper them along with the actors.

On the tenth night comes the festival of Dussehra. A giant figure of Ravana stands at the edge of the field. When the play reaches the battle, the figure is set alight. Fireworks burst overhead, and the crowd cheers.
An old man in the crowd has watched this play every year since he was a boy. "It is the same story," he says, smiling. "And it is new every time." Then he joins in the cheering.
story.think: Why might people want to watch the same story every year?

lessons.title: Sita in Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: In Lanka, Sita stays strong and refuses Ravana.
reading: Ravana carries Sita to his island kingdom of *Lanka*. He keeps her in a garden of ashoka trees. He wants her to marry him. He offers her riches and a palace.
Sita refuses him every time. She stays loyal to Rama. The poem shows her as brave and strong, even though she is far from home and all alone. She waits for Rama to come.
Many Hindus honor Sita as a goddess and a model of courage and faithfulness. Some readers today also see her as a strong woman who says no to a powerful king.

words.d: Ravana's island kingdom in the Ramayana
staying true to someone

look.title: Sita Says No
look.text: Ravana boasts of his riches and power. Sita places a blade of grass between them and speaks to him without fear. She tells him she belongs to Rama and warns him to return her.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Book 5)
look.prompt: What does Sita's answer show about her?

check.q: Where does Ravana keep Sita?
check.why: Sita is held in a garden of ashoka trees in Lanka.

check.q: What does Sita do when Ravana asks her to marry him?
check.why: Sita refuses Ravana every time.

check.q: How do many Hindus honor Sita?
choices: As a goddess and a model of courage
check.why: Many Hindus honor Sita as a goddess and a model of courage.

lessons.title: Hanuman's Journey
lessons.mainIdea: Hanuman leaps to Lanka, finds Sita and brings back word to Rama.
reading: Rama makes friends with Sugriva, king of the monkey people, called the *vanaras*. Sugriva's wise minister, Hanuman, becomes Rama's most devoted helper.
Sundara Kanda tells how Hanuman leaps across the ocean to Lanka. He searches the city at night. At last he finds Sita and gives her Rama's ring as a sign.
Hanuman is caught, and his tail is set on fire. He escapes and spreads the fire across Lanka. Then he leaps back to Rama with the good news. Many Hindus pray to Hanuman for strength and courage.

words.d: one of the monkey people who help Rama
the king of the vanaras and Rama's ally

look.title: A Hero in Many Homes
look.text: In many Hindu homes in Illinois, a small picture of Hanuman hangs near the door. Some families chant the Hanuman Chalisa, a 40-verse hymn in Hindi by tradition credited to Tulsidas, on Tuesdays.
look.prompt: What qualities of Hanuman might a family want to remember each day?

check.q: Who is Sugriva?
check.why: Sugriva is king of the monkey people and Rama's ally.

check.q: What does Hanuman give Sita?
check.why: Hanuman gives Sita Rama's ring as a sign.

check.q: Which kanda tells Hanuman's journey?
check.why: Sundara Kanda, Book 5, follows Hanuman.

lessons.title: The Bridge to Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: Rama's army builds a bridge across the sea, and Ravana's brother joins Rama.
reading: Rama's army reaches the ocean. How can they cross? The poem says a vanara named Nala leads the building of a great bridge of rocks and trees across the sea.
Folk tellings add a little squirrel who helps with grains of sand. It is not in Valmiki's poem, but many families love it. It shows that every helper counts.
Before the battle, Ravana's brother Vibhishana leaves Lanka. He tells Ravana to return Sita, but Ravana will not listen. Vibhishana joins Rama, who welcomes him.

words.d: Ravana's brother, who leaves Lanka and joins Rama
a story passed on by ordinary people, often by telling

look.title: Choosing a Side
look.text: Vibhishana is Ravana's own brother. He loves his family. But he believes Ravana is doing wrong by keeping Sita. He warns his brother, then leaves to join Rama.
look.prompt: Was Vibhishana's choice hard? Why?

check.q: Who leads the building of the bridge in Valmiki's poem?
check.why: The poem says the vanara Nala led the building.

check.q: Is the squirrel story part of Valmiki's poem?
choices: No, it comes from the Rig Veda
No, it is a folk telling
check.why: The squirrel is a well-loved folk addition.

check.q: Who is Vibhishana?
check.why: Vibhishana leaves Ravana and joins Rama.

lessons.title: The Battle
lessons.mainIdea: Rama defeats Ravana in a great battle and frees Sita.
reading: Yuddha Kanda, the "book of battle," tells of a long war in Lanka. Many warriors fight on both sides. Lakshmana is badly hurt, and Hanuman flies to bring healing herbs from a mountain.
At last Rama faces Ravana himself. The fight is long and hard. Rama wins. Many Hindus remember this victory as good winning over evil. The long war is over at last.
After the battle, Rama makes Vibhishana the new king of Lanka. He does not take Lanka for himself. The poem also shows respect for Ravana's funeral rites.

words.d: the sixth book of the Ramayana, telling the battle
winning a battle or contest

look.title: Hanuman and the Mountain
look.text: Lakshmana lies wounded. Hanuman must find a healing herb on a far mountain. He cannot tell which plant it is. So, the story says, he lifts the whole mountaintop and carries it back to the battlefield.
look.prompt: What does this scene show about Hanuman's loyalty?

check.q: What does Yuddha Kanda tell about?
check.why: Yuddha Kanda is the book of battle.

check.q: Who does Rama make king of Lanka?
check.why: Rama makes Vibhishana king and does not take Lanka.

check.q: What do many Hindus see in Rama's victory?
check.why: Many Hindus remember it as good winning over evil.

lessons.title: Coming Home
lessons.mainIdea: Rama returns to Ayodhya and is crowned king, and many Hindus remember this at Diwali.
reading: The fourteen years are over. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana fly home to Ayodhya in a flying chariot. Hanuman goes ahead to tell Bharata the news. The chariot is called Pushpaka.
Bharata gives back the kingdom joyfully. Rama is crowned king at last, with Sita as queen. The people of Ayodhya celebrate. There is music and feasting in every street.
Many Hindus remember this homecoming at Diwali, the festival of lights, when they light lamps to welcome Rama and Sita. Others remember Lakshmi or Krishna at Diwali.

words.d: made king or queen in a ceremony
returning home after being away

look.title: Lamps in Every Window
look.text: Picture Ayodhya on the night Rama returns. Rows of lamps glow on rooftops and doorsteps. Music plays. Bharata runs to meet his brother. Many Hindus light diyas at Diwali to remember this night.
look.prompt: How does the story connect to what families do at Diwali?

check.q: How long was Rama away?
check.why: Rama returns after fourteen years.

check.q: What does Bharata do when Rama returns?
check.why: Bharata happily returns the kingdom.

check.q: Which festival do many Hindus connect with Rama's return?
check.why: Many Hindus light Diwali lamps to remember Rama's return.

lessons.title: Rama Rajya
lessons.mainIdea: Rama Rajya, "the rule of Rama," is an ideal of fair and peaceful government.
reading: The poem says Rama ruled with fairness for many years. People were safe, fields were full and no one was treated unjustly. This is called *Rama Rajya*, "the rule of Rama."
Over time, Rama Rajya became an ideal, a picture of what good government could be. Mahatma Gandhi used the phrase for a fair India where the poorest people were cared for.
Others have used the phrase in different ways, and people still debate what it should mean. Many Hindus use it simply to mean a kind and just ruler. Its meaning is still discussed.

words.d: "the rule of Rama"; an ideal of fair and peaceful government
a picture of the best way something could be

look.title: What Makes a Good Ruler?
look.text: Imagine your class gets to design a fair leader. Would the leader listen to everyone? Help people who have less? Keep promises? Treat people equally? Many readers of the Ramayana ask the same questions.

lessons.title: Hard Questions About Sita
lessons.mainIdea: Readers ask hard questions about how Sita is treated, and they answer in different ways.
reading: After the battle, Valmiki's poem says Rama doubts Sita, because she lived in Ravana's kingdom. Sita walks into a fire to prove she is pure, and the fire god, Agni, returns her unharmed.
In the last book, Uttara Kanda, Rama sends Sita away because people gossip about her. She raises their twin sons in Valmiki's forest home. Many readers find these parts very painful.

Readers answer in different ways. Some explain Rama's choices as a king's duty. Some say these parts were added later. Many retellings, including women's songs, tell the story from Sita's side and question Rama.

words.d: the seventh and last book of the Ramayana
the fire god in Hindu texts

look.title: Three Readers, One Passage
look.text: Reader 1: Rama had to put his kingdom's trust first. Reader 2: Many scholars think this book was added later. Reader 3: The women's songs I grew up with take Sita's side and ask why she was treated this way.
look.prompt: How can readers who love the same story still disagree about it?

lessons.title: Sita's Side of the Story
lessons.mainIdea: Many tellings, including women's songs and a Bengali Ramayana by a woman poet, put Sita at the center.
reading: For centuries, women in Indian villages have sung their own Ramayana songs. They sing them while working, at weddings and at festivals. Many of these songs focus on Sita's feelings.
In the 1500s, the poet Chandrabati wrote a Ramayana in Bengali. She was one of the first women known to retell the story. Her telling puts Sita's sorrow at the center.
Scholars say there are many Ramayanas, not just one. Each telling reflects its place, its people and its questions. This variety is part of why the story stays alive.

words.d: the point of view from which a story is told
a woman poet who wrote a Bengali Ramayana in the 1500s

look.title: Same Event, New Eyes
look.text: Tell the golden deer part twice. First as Rama sees it: a strange deer, a task for his wife. Then as Sita sees it: a lovely creature, a wish, and then fear and loneliness when she is taken.
look.prompt: How does the feeling of the story change when you switch perspective?

check.why: Many women's songs center on Sita.

check.q: What do scholars mean by "many Ramayanas"?

check.why: Scholars point to many tellings across places and times.

lessons.title: The Ramayana Across Asia
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana traveled to Southeast Asia, where it has its own tellings.
reading: Traders, teachers and travelers carried the Ramayana beyond India. In Thailand it became the *Ramakien*. In Cambodia it is the Reamker. In Indonesia, a Javanese poem tells it too.
These tellings keep the main story but change details. In the Ramakien, Hanuman has a bigger, more playful role. Dancers act out scenes in masks and golden costumes.
The great temple of Angkor Wat in Cambodia has stone carvings of the Ramayana battle. In Indonesia, many Muslims enjoy Ramayana puppet shows and dances as part of their culture.

words.d: the Thai telling of the Ramayana
the arts, beliefs and ways of life of a group of people

check.why: In Indonesia the Ramayana is part of shared culture, enjoyed by many Muslims too.

lessons.title: Ramlila: The Story on Stage
lessons.mainIdea: In the Ramlila, towns act out the Ramayana, often over many nights before Dussehra.
reading: The *Ramlila* is a play of Rama's life. Towns across North India perform it each autumn, often over about ten nights. Many performances follow Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.
It usually ends at Dussehra, the festival of Rama's victory. In many places, huge figures of Ravana are burned. Crowds cheer as good wins over evil. Fireworks light up the sky.
In 2005, UNESCO honored the Ramlila as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Some Hindu communities in Illinois hold their own Ramlila plays.

words.d: a play of Rama's life, often performed over many nights
the festival that celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana

look.title: The Victory the Play Celebrates
look.text: At the end of the long battle, Rama defeats Ravana. The gods rejoice, and Rama's allies celebrate.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Book 6)
look.prompt: Why might a play end on this moment?
